lead: Embedded C keeps the C language you know but ties every byte to the 8051's fixed memory and registers. A program that would run on a PC must be told which names are special function registers, which variables a hardware interrupt can change, and where variables live. The compiler then turns the source into a HEX file for program flash. This style is used for small control tasks: reading a key on P1, timing a pulse with Timer 0, sending a byte on the UART, or blinking an LED from an interrupt.
prereq: You need: 4.2 for port latches, 4.3 for timer modes, 4.4 for SBUF and baud rate, and 4.5 for vectors and IE/IP.

blocks.text: Standard C has no idea that address 0x90 is Port 1. Embedded C adds a small set of keywords so the programmer can name hardware. The C51 compiler from Keil and the free SDCC compiler both accept this idea; exact keyword spelling can differ, so check the header. The source file is compiled and linked into a HEX file, which a programmer writes into the 8051's program flash. Some syllabi call this C51 programming or 8051 C programming.

Choose data types by size, not habit. On C51, unsigned char is 8 bits (0 to 255), unsigned int is 16 bits (0 to 65535), and bit is one bit. A port byte, a counter below 256, or a bit mask should be unsigned char. Use unsigned int only for values that need more than 8 bits, such as a 16-bit timer count or a delay loop count. This saves data memory and code space.

A special function register (SFR) is declared with sfr and its byte address. For example, sfr P1 = 0x90; tells the compiler that the name P1 is the byte at address 0x90. A single pin is declared with sbit: sbit LED = P1^0; means bit 0 of P1. Most projects include a vendor header such as reg51.h instead of writing these lines by hand. The header also declares IE, IP, TMOD, SCON and SBUF.

Use bitwise operators to change selected bits without disturbing the rest. Set bits with OR: P1 = P1 | 0x09; sets bit 0 and bit 3. Clear bits with AND plus NOT: P1 = P1 & ~0x7F; clears bits 0 to 6 and leaves bit 7. Toggle bits with XOR: P2 = P2 ^ 0x04; flips bit 2. The symbol ~ is bitwise NOT; & is bitwise AND. Do not confuse & with logical &&.

A variable changed outside normal flow must be volatile. An interrupt service routine (ISR), a hardware register, or another task can change it between two reads. Without volatile, the compiler may keep the value in a register and never reload memory. Example: volatile unsigned char ticks; then ticks++; inside the Timer 0 ISR and if (ticks >= 10) in main.

items: sfr names a byte at an address.
sbit names one bit of an SFR or bit-addressable RAM.
volatile forces a fresh read from memory.
Use parentheses around mixed bitwise expressions.

blocks.text: The 8051 has several data spaces, and the compiler must choose where variables go. The small model puts variables in internal RAM (data), which is fast but only about 128 bytes. The compact model uses one 256-byte page of external RAM (pdata), addressed through a pointer. The large model uses up to 64 KB of external RAM (xdata), which is slower and needs 16-bit pointers. Small and compact models are faster than the large model: small-model data is reached with direct and register addressing, and compact-model data uses 8-bit pointers into one page. The large model needs 16-bit pointers and external-memory (MOVX) cycles; keeping data out of xdata also leaves internal RAM free for the stack. The stack sits in internal RAM and grows upward; deep recursion or large local arrays can overflow it.

Port program: P1 = 0x0F; writes 0000 1111 to Port 1. To make P1.0 an input, set only that pin's latch to 1: P1 = P1 | 0x01; then read P1.0. Every pin must have latch 1 before it is used as an input; see 4.2. Timer 0 program in C: TMOD = 0x01; TH0 = 0xFC; TL0 = 0x18; TR0 = 1; while (!TF0); TF0 = 0; This uses mode 1, 16-bit timer, and waits for overflow. Serial program: SCON = 0x50; TMOD = 0x20; TH1 = 0xFD; TR1 = 1; SBUF = 'A'; while (!TI); TI = 0; This sets mode 1 UART with Timer 1 mode 2 baud rate. Interrupt program: volatile unsigned char ticks; void timer0_isr(void) interrupt 1 { TH0 = 0xFC; TL0 = 0x18; ticks++; } void main(void) { TMOD = 0x01; TH0 = 0xFC; TL0 = 0x18; ET0 = 1; EA = 1; TR0 = 1; while (1) { } } Mode 1 has no auto-reload, so the ISR must write TH0 and TL0 again for every 1000-count interval. The Timer 0 vector is 1 in C51; check your compiler header for exact syntax.

examples.question: Port 1 holds 0xA5 and Port 2 holds 0x00. Execute these two C statements on an 8051: P1 = (P1 | 0x09) & 0x7F; P2 ^= 0x04; Give P1 and P2 after both statements, in hex and decimal.
examples.answer: After both statements, P1 = 0x2D (45 decimal) and P2 = 0x04 (4 decimal).
examples.check:
p1 = 0xA5
p2 = 0x00
p1 = (p1 | 0x09) & 0x7F
p2 ^= 0x04
print(p1)
print(p2)

traps: Do not assume int is 32 bits. On C51 int is usually 16 bits; a 32-bit value costs more code and time.
A variable changed by an ISR must be volatile, or the compiler may cache it and the main loop never sees the change.

sbit declares one bit; sfr declares a whole byte. An sbit can be declared only for a bit-addressable SFR (address ending in 0x0 or 0x8) or for bit-addressable RAM. TMOD (0x89) and SBUF (0x99) cannot have an sbit name; to change one bit of TMOD, mask the byte with bitwise operators.
The small memory model is fast but has little space. Large arrays in data can overflow the 8051 stack or leave no room for locals.
Use & for bit masking and && for logical AND; the same trap exists for | and ||.

quiz.q: On C51, how many bits are in unsigned char and unsigned int?
quiz.a: unsigned char is 8 bits (0 to 255). unsigned int is 16 bits (0 to 65535).

quiz.q: Why must a variable changed by an ISR be declared volatile?
quiz.a: The compiler may keep it in a register and reuse that copy. volatile forces each read to come from memory, so the main code sees the ISR's change.

quiz.q: P1 = 0x3C. What is P1 after P1 = P1 | 0x03; and then P1 = P1 & ~0x0F;?
quiz.a: 0x3C | 0x03 = 0x3F. Then ~0x0F has low byte 0xF0, and 0x3F & 0xF0 = 0x30. Final P1 = 0x30.

quiz.q: Write one C line that toggles bit 5 of P2 without changing other bits.
A C51 program declares unsigned int i; and uses for (i=0; i<70000; i++);. Explain what goes wrong.
quiz.a: On C51 unsigned int is 16 bits, so i wraps from 65535 to 0. It never reaches 70000, and the loop continues forever unless another condition stops it.

quiz.q: Why can the large memory model be slower than the small model on the 8051?
quiz.a: Large-model variables live in xdata, reached by 16-bit pointers and external-memory cycles. Small-model data lives in internal RAM with direct and register addressing, so it needs fewer machine cycles.
It declares LED as bit 0 of the SFR P1. Writing LED changes only P1.0; reading LED returns that one bit.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern 8051 tools still use this model: Keil C51 and SDCC generate code for small memory models, and vendor headers hide SFR addresses. In industry, the same ideas appear as memory-mapped I/O in ARM Cortex-M headers, where volatile pointers replace sfr. Search for "SDCC 8051 memory models", "Keil C51 sfr sbit", and "volatile interrupt variable" to go further. The next step is Unit 6, where ARM C uses similar volatile rules but a 32-bit flat address space.
